english: Minkowski conjectures the theorem that a closed surface made of ideally flexible but non-stretchable material cannot be bent in without acquiring creases, i.e. cannot be continuously deformed by bending; in particular this holds for the sphere.
topic: Three short notes: Minkowski's conjecture that a closed surface of flexible but inextensible material cannot be continuously bent (especially the sphere); whether all ruler-and-compass constructions can be done with compass alone; and a task to prove that no number in the cyclotomic field other than the root of unity has discriminant equal to the field discriminant.

triage.modern_statement: Rigidity of closed surfaces under isometric deformation. Is a closed surface S in R^3 rigid, in the sense that every continuous family of isometric deformations of S (bendings that keep all intrinsic lengths fixed) is just a rigid motion? Minkowski's conjecture asks this in particular for the round sphere. The natural general version, which the note suggests, asks it for closed convex surfaces (ovaloids). The broader version asks it for arbitrary closed surfaces. The answer depends on the smoothness class: the classical results concern smooth or analytic surfaces, and polyhedral surfaces are a separate case.
triage.answered_by: The sphere case is Liebmann's theorem: the sphere is rigid. Liebmann proved it around 1899–1900, close to the time of this diary entry, but the date and paper title were not checked against the sources found here. For closed convex surfaces with positive curvature (ovaloids), Cohn-Vossen proved rigidity in 1927 for analytic surfaces and extended it to C^3 surfaces in 1936. Herglotz gave a short proof in 1943, and Wintner and Sacksteder later weakened the smoothness assumptions. For non-convex closed surfaces the general statement is false for polyhedra: Connelly (1977) built a non-self-intersecting flexible closed polyhedral surface, disproving the rigidity conjecture for polyhedra. Cohn-Vossen (1929) also studied closed surfaces that admit nontrivial isometric mappings.

evidence.claim: Liebmann's theorem states that the sphere is rigid.

Cohn-Vossen proved his first rigidity result in 1927 for positively curved analytic surfaces and extended it to C^3 surfaces in 1936. The standard textbook proof is Herglotz's 1943 integral-formula argument, and Wintner and Sacksteder later extended the result.

Cohn-Vossen's 1927 paper 'Two propositions' proved rigidity of ovaloids (closed convex surfaces with positive curvature everywhere), and his 1929 paper 'Nonrigid closed surfaces' studied closed surfaces that admit nontrivial isometric mappings.
Cohn-Vossen's rigidity work developed Cauchy's study of convex polyhedra and was continued by A. D. Aleksandrov and A. V. Pogorelov.
Connelly (1977) constructed the first non-self-intersecting flexible closed polyhedral surface, disproving the rigidity conjecture for polyhedra.

triage.why: The sphere case Minkowski conjectured is settled by Liebmann's theorem. The convex generalization was settled by Cohn-Vossen (1927/1936) and later refined, and the sources show that rigidity and flexible polyhedra are still being studied (2020 IMRN paper, 2025 arXiv paper). I could not find a source that explicitly credits this conjecture to Minkowski, so linking this diary note to Liebmann's theorem is my identification, not something a source states. I also did not check Liebmann's exact publication. The note's wording, 'without acquiring creases', points to a smoothness condition. That fits the known fact that non-smooth (C^1) isometric deformations behave very differently, but my searches did not get as far as finding a source for that. I also did not confirm, beyond the general statement that the field is active, whether rigidity of smooth non-convex closed surfaces is still open. This note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems.
